italian-game.explanation: Ng5 looks aggressive targeting f7, but after d5! exd5 Na5, Black wins the bishop pair and has a strong center. Instead c3 prepares d4 for a sound central build-up.
italian-game.shortNarration: c3 — prepare d4, build the centre

italian-game.explanation: Playing d4 immediately is premature — after exd4 cxd4 Bb4, Black pins the knight and puts pressure on d4. First develop with Nbd2, preparing d4 with proper support.
italian-game.shortNarration: Nbd2 — support d4 before pushing it

italian-game.explanation: Bxf7+ wins a pawn but after Kxf7, Black gets the bishop pair and the king is safe on g8 after Rf8. Develop solidly with d3 instead.
italian-game.shortNarration: d3 — develop solidly, skip the sac

french-defence.explanation: After e5 the f6-knight is attacked and must move — …c5 ignores it and simply drops the piece to exf6. First retreat the knight to d7 to reorganize, then strike the base with …c5 once it is safely prepared.
french-defence.shortNarration: Nfd7 — save the attacked knight first

french-defence.explanation: …Nf6 here just invites e5, kicking the knight back and handing White free space. …d5 is the whole point of the French — challenge the e4-pawn at once and fight for the centre.

caro-kann.explanation: e6 locks in the light-squared bishop — the Caro-Kann's main advantage is developing this bishop OUTSIDE the pawn chain first. Bf5 is the whole point of the opening.
caro-kann.shortNarration: Bf5 — bishop out before locking with e6

caro-kann.explanation: f3 weakens the kingside and blocks the knight. Nc3 develops naturally and maintains pressure on d5.
caro-kann.shortNarration: Nc3 — develop, keep pressure on d5

caro-kann.explanation: Nxe4 walks into Nxe4 dxe4 Qd4 forking e4 and g7. Simply recapture with dxe4 keeping a solid position.

ruy-lopez.explanation: Nf6 allows 4. O-O Nxe4 5. d4 (the Open Ruy Lopez) which leads to very sharp tactical play favoring White. a6 forces the bishop back and gives Black more flexibility.
ruy-lopez.shortNarration: a6 — question the bishop, stay flexible

qgd.explanation: Taking on c4 too early (QGA) lets White develop freely with e3+Bxc4. In the QGD, e6 maintains the central tension and keeps a solid pawn structure.
Bb4 pins the knight but after Qa4+ Nc6 e3, the bishop is awkwardly placed. Be7 is the classical move, developing solidly and preparing to castle.

kings-indian-defence.explanation: Playing e5 immediately runs into d5 closing the center when White is better prepared. Play d6 first to support e5, which typically comes after O-O and proper piece placement.
Bg4 pins the knight but after Be3 the pin is not effective and Black wastes time. e5 is the key KID break, contesting central control.
exd4 opens the center which favors White. Nh5 prepares f5 for the classic KID kingside attack.

london-system.explanation: Defending b2 passively with b3 weakens the queenside and concedes the initiative. Nc3 develops with tempo — the pawn is taboo, since ...Qxb2 runs into Na4 trapping the queen.
london-system.shortNarration: Nc3 — develop, the pawn is taboo

london-system.explanation: Trading the prized London bishop with Bxd6 hands Black comfortable equality. Bg3 preserves it, keeping the grip on the b8-h2 diagonal — the soul of the whole system.
Ignoring the attack on the bishop with a move like Be2 lets ...Nxf4 trade off the prized London bishop for a knight. Bg5 keeps it active and out of harm's way.

english-opening.explanation: Grabbing the pawn with Nxe5 walks into ...Nxc3! — the d5-knight forks the queen and White loses material. Just fianchetto with Bg2; the reversed Sicilian is about pressure, not pawn-grabbing.
Drifting with d3 keeps the symmetry and lets Black equalize comfortably. d4 is the thematic break that shatters the mirror and hands White the initiative his extra tempo earns.
english-opening.shortNarration: d4 — break the symmetry, don't drift

english-opening.explanation: Releasing with cxd5 exd5 gives Black free, easy development. e5 is the whole point of the Mikenas — gain space and kick the f6-knight, keeping the initiative.
english-opening.shortNarration: e5 — push past, keep the initiative

sicilian-dragon.explanation: a5 is premature queenside expansion before castling. O-O gets the king safe first — in the Dragon, a single tempo can decide the game.
sicilian-dragon.shortNarration: O-O first — king safe before a5.

sicilian-dragon.explanation: Be6 allows Nxe6 fxe6 with a weakened pawn structure. Qa5 starts immediate queenside counterplay which is critical in the Yugoslav Attack.

scandinavian-defence.explanation: Playing …e6 first locks the light-squared bishop behind its own pawn — the very French problem the Scandinavian exists to avoid. Develop …Bf5 (or …Bg4) FIRST, getting the bishop outside the chain, and only then play …e6.

…Qe5+ is a greedy check that goes nowhere: after Be2 the bishop blocks calmly and Black has only misplaced the queen and blocked the e-pawn. …Qa5 keeps the queen active and out of harm's way, the sound main-line square.
scandinavian-defence.shortNarration: Qa5 — active retreat, not the greedy check

scandinavian-defence.explanation: Shuffling the queen to b6 wastes a tempo and lets White keep the extra d5-pawn. Just recapture with …Nxd5, regaining the pawn and centralising the knight — equal and easy.

catalan-opening.explanation: Lunging after the c4-pawn with Na3 wastes time and misplaces the knight on the rim. Nf3 develops naturally — White recovers the pawn later with the bishop pair and long-diagonal pressure.
Qxc4 loses the queen to ...bxc4 — the b5-pawn guards c4! Undermine the base of the chain with b3 instead, recovering the pawn under far better circumstances.
Releasing the tension with cxd5 hands Black an easy game and a clear structure. Keep the tension and prepare the thematic e4-break with Nbd2 — that is how White plays for the advantage.

slav-defence.explanation: Premature capture on c4 without preparation allows White to recapture easily and gain a strong center. Developing Nf6 first maintains tension and follows sound Slav principles.
Bg4 pins the knight but allows the sharp Slav Exchange where White plays Ne5 with tempo on the bishop. Playing e6 solidifies the center and prepares Bd6 or Bb4 with a sound position.

nimzo-indian.explanation: When a3 questions the bishop, retreating …Be7 throws away the whole point of the Nimzo — two tempi lost and the pin abandoned for nothing. Take with …Bxc3+: damage White's structure (or, in the Qc2 line, loosen the grip on e4) and play on from there. The bishop is meant to be traded, not retreated.
nimzo-indian.shortNarration: Bxc3+ — take, don't retreat the bishop

nimzo-indian.explanation: Trading …Bxc3+ here, before White has spent a3 to force it, hands over the bishop pair for free — White recaptures with the b-pawn and is happy to have the centre and the bishops. Keep the pin and strike with …d5, contesting the centre while the bishop still does its job.
nimzo-indian.shortNarration: d5 — keep the pin, strike the centre

grunfeld-defence.explanation: Exchanging on c3 helps White recapture and strengthen the center without any compensation. Playing c5 immediately strikes at the d4 pawn, generating counterplay on the dark squares as is typical in the Grunfeld.
grunfeld-defence.shortNarration: …c5 — hit the centre, time the trade.

grunfeld-defence.explanation: Retreating with 5...Nb6 hands White exactly what the Grünfeld is built to attack: a big, unchallenged e4/d4 centre and a free game. The whole point is 5...Nxc3 6.bxc3 — fracturing White's queenside pawns — and only THEN besieging the centre with ...Bg7, ...c5 and ...Nc6. Trade on c3 first; don't retreat.
grunfeld-defence.shortNarration: Nxc3 first; Nb6 gives White the centre

scotch-game.explanation: Nxd4 Nxd4 exd4 leaves Black with an isolated d-pawn and no compensation. exd4 Nxd4 gives Black active piece play.
scotch-game.shortNarration: exd4 — recapture for active piece play

scotch-game.explanation: Nxe4 loses to d5 forking the knight and bishop. Bd6 attacks the knight and develops naturally.
e5 pushes the pawn forward without support and the knight retreats to safety. Bd3 develops calmly with a lead in development.
scotch-game.shortNarration: Bd3 — develop calmly, keep your lead

vienna-game.explanation: Bc5 is passive and allows f4 with tempo. Nf6 counter-attacks e4 and fights for the initiative.
vienna-game.shortNarration: Nf6 — hit e4, take the initiative

vienna-game.explanation: exf4 gives up the center. d5 strikes back centrally and opens lines for development.
vienna-game.shortNarration: d5 — strike back in the centre

vienna-game.explanation: fxe5 Nxe4 gives Black active piece play. d3 solidifies the center and prepares calm development.
vienna-game.shortNarration: d3 — hold the centre, develop calmly

four-knights-game.explanation: Nxe5 is the Halloween Gambit — a knight sacrifice that is objectively unsound; with accurate defence Black is simply better. Bb5 keeps the principled Spanish Four Knights, pressuring the c6-knight and preparing the d4 break.
four-knights-game.shortNarration: Bb5 — the sound Spanish, not the gambit

four-knights-game.explanation: Grabbing the pawn with Nxe5 invites the strong ...Qe7, when Black regains it with a fine game — and the careless f4 even drops a piece to ...Nxb5. Be2 is the calm Maroczy retreat that keeps the bishop pair and a sound edge.
four-knights-game.shortNarration: Be2 — don't grab e5, retreat calmly

four-knights-game.explanation: Drifting with a slow move like h3 lets Black comfortably hold the symmetry. Bg5 breaks it on White's terms, pinning the f6-knight — which Black cannot mirror without wrecking his own kingside.
four-knights-game.shortNarration: Bg5 — break the symmetry, pin f6

sicilian-alapin.explanation: e6 is too passive and lets White build a big centre with d4. d5 challenges White's centre at once and gives Black the freer game.
sicilian-alapin.shortNarration: d5 — challenge now, not passive e6.

sicilian-alapin.explanation: Qxd4 grabs a pawn but loses time after Nc3, when the queen is chased back and White races ahead in development. Nf6 develops with tempo and eyes e4.
sicilian-alapin.shortNarration: Nf6 — develop; Qxd4 just loses time.

pirc-defence.explanation: ...e5 cracks the d-file open under Black's own queen — White plays dxe5 dxe5 Qxd8+ and the queens trade off with check, costing Black the right to castle. Nf6 develops naturally and pressures e4 in true Pirc style.

punishmentLine.title: Why ...e5 loses on the spot
annotations: ...e5 looks like a fight for the centre, but d6 was just played last move and no longer defends e5. The d-file is one trade away from cracking wide open with Black's queen still sitting on d8.
White takes immediately. dxe5 is forced — anything else loses a pawn for nothing.
Black recaptures with the d6-pawn — the only way to keep material — and the d-file flies open from d1 all the way to d8. The white queen now stares straight at Black's queen with nothing in between.
Qxd8+ — queens trade with check. There is no recapture except with the king.
The king takes back on d8 and Black has lost the right to castle forever. Down zero material, but the hypermodern Pirc just lost its quiet middlegame future. Game basically over before move five.

pirc-defence.explanation: ...Bg4 develops the bishop with a pin, but it's premature — White just kicks with h3 and Black has to give up the bishop pair on f3 with no compensation. Castling first keeps the queen's bishop in reserve for a square where it actually does something.

punishmentLine.title: Why ...Bg4 gives up the bishop pair
annotations: ...Bg4 pins the f3-knight to the queen, looking aggressive. The problem: the bishop has no safe retreat once h3 hits it, and the c8-bishop is the Pirc's most valuable long-term piece for the slow manoeuvring middlegame.
h3 — the simple kick. Retreats to h5 lose to g4, retreats to d7 or c8 just waste two tempi.
...Bxf3 is forced. Black gives up the light-squared bishop for the knight — the bishop pair is gone, and with it the Pirc's long-term endgame chances.
Qxf3 — White recaptures with the queen, now centralised and eyeing both b7 and f7. White has the bishop pair, a flexible centre, and Black has no real compensation for the structural concession.

pirc-defence.shortNarration: O-O — castle, keep the bishop in reserve

pirc-defence.explanation: ...c5 invites White to slam the centre shut with d5, leaving the c8-bishop dead behind the c5/d6/e7 pawn chain and the g7-bishop biting on a closed wall. Bg4 first pins the f3-knight and creates real tension before White can consolidate.

punishmentLine.title: Why ...c5 locks YOU out of the game
annotations: ...c5 looks like Pirc-style counterplay, hitting d4. But White's centre is fully supported — d4 isn't dropping — and the push lets White close the door instead of opening it.
d5 — and that's the trap. The centre is locked tight; ...c5 can't be undone. The c8-bishop is now buried behind c7-c5 with nowhere to go, and the g7-bishop bites on a wall at d4-e5.
...Na6 — the knight has to come out somewhere, but with the centre closed there are no good squares. The c7-square is the only home and even there the knight does nothing.

Nd2 — White reroutes calmly to better squares (f1, g3, then maybe f5) knowing Black has no plan. Closed centre, all of Black's pieces with no scope — this is the slow, suffocating defeat the Pirc is supposed to AVOID.

pirc-defence.shortNarration: Bg4 — pin the knight, make tension first

evans-gambit.explanation: Grabbing the pawn back with Nxe5 throws away the whole point of the gambit. d4! builds the towering centre and keeps the initiative — that is exactly what the b-pawn bought.
evans-gambit.shortNarration: d4 — build the centre, keep the attack

evans-gambit.explanation: In the Compromised Defence, meekly regaining the pawn with Nxc3 lets Black consolidate the extra material. Qb3! is the point — the queen and bishop train on f7 and the attack roars on, worth far more than a pawn.
evans-gambit.shortNarration: Qb3 — train on f7, not the pawn

kings-gambit.explanation: 2…d5 (Falkbeer Counter-Gambit) is sharp but theoretically dubious for Black at the top level. After 3.exd5 e4 White has the Nimzowitsch Variation 4.d3 with a strong reply. Accepting the gambit with 2…exf4 is the principled move — keep the extra pawn and defend.
kings-gambit.shortNarration: exf4 — take it, hold the extra pawn

kings-gambit.explanation: 4.h3 is engine-equivalent but wastes a critical tempo near your own king. 4.Bc4 develops with two threats: it eyes f7 AND prepares O-O immediately. In gambit play tempo is the gambit — every wasted move gives Black time to consolidate the extra pawn into a fortress. Practical edge: with Bc4 you reach an attacking middlegame; with h3 you reach an equal-but-passive middlegame.
kings-gambit.shortNarration: Bc4 — develop with tempo, hit f7

kings-gambit.explanation: Qh4+ is engine-fine — White just plays Kf1 and the king gets to g1 next move anyway. But the queen on h4 is OFFSIDE: it commits early and gives White moves like Nf3, Nc3, d4 with tempo on the queen. 3…Nf6 develops a piece (zero tempo cost) and prepares …d5 to challenge the center. Practical edge: with Nf6 you have more pieces in play when the center opens.
kings-gambit.shortNarration: Nf6 — develop, don't chase with the queen

petrov-defence.explanation: 3…Nxe4?? is the most famous beginner blunder in the Petrov. After 4.Qe2 Nf6 5.Nc6+ (revealing the discovered attack on the queen) White wins material. The correct 3…d6 kicks the knight first; only THEN 4…Nxe4 is safe.

Cochrane Gambit — both 4…Kxf7 and 4…Qe7 are theoretically sound, but Kxf7 commits the king to a permanently exposed life: it cannot castle and must shuffle to safety by hand. 4…Qe7 keeps the king safe and hits the offside f7-knight, reaching a normal middlegame up material.

queens-gambit.explanation: 4…h6 spends a tempo on the wing before developing — after 5.Bxf6 Qxf6 White completes development with a small edge while Black's light-squared bishop is still hemmed in behind the e6-pawn. The mainline 4…Be7 develops and breaks the pin, so the f6-knight is no longer tied to the queen.

qga.explanation: Defending the extra pawn with 3…b5? is a known trap — White plays 4.a4 b4 5.b3 cxb3 6.axb5 with a huge attack on the open files. The principled move is 3…Nf6 — give back the pawn for development and play a normal QGA position.

Even after the bishop recaptures, …b5? is still a structural mistake — White plays 6.Bd3 and Black has weakened the queenside permanently. The mainline 5…c5 fights for the center and prepares …Nc6 development.
Pushing 2…e5? loses a pawn after 3.dxe5 d4 4.Nf3 Nc6 5.a3 with a clearly favorable position for White. The QGA accepts with 2…dxc4 — clean and theoretically sound.

sicilian-sveshnikov.explanation: Playing a6 too early walks into Nd6+ — after Bxd6 Qxd6 White grabs the bishop pair and wrecks Black's structure. d6 first defends the e5-pawn while keeping the knight kicked.
After Nf3 (avoiding the mainline Ndb5), d5 overextends and loses the e-pawn structure. d6 is solid and similar in spirit to the Najdorf.

semi-slav.explanation: 6…Bb4 is fine in Nimzo-Indian setups but in Semi-Slav it lets White play 7.O-O dxc4 8.Bxc4 with extra tempo. The Meran starts with 6…dxc4 7.Bxc4 b5 immediately.

5…h6 is engine-equivalent but pedagogically lazy — White plays 6.Bh4 keeping the pin and Black has spent a tempo on a non-developing pawn move. The Botvinnik 5…dxc4 immediately commits to the sharpest fight: White will get something for the pin (e4 + Nxg5 sacrifice), Black gets the bishop pair + queenside expansion. Practical edge: with dxc4 you reach the position you wanted; with h6 you waste a move and White still has the pin.

reti-opening.explanation: 2.e3 is passive and surrenders the Réti's whole point. 2.c4 immediately challenges the d5-pawn from the flank — the hypermodern idea that controls the centre without occupying it.
reti-opening.shortNarration: c4 — challenge d5 from the flank

reti-opening.explanation: Drifting with a slow move like a3 lets Black consolidate comfortably. cxd5 opens the long diagonal for the g2-bishop and the c-file — the thematic Réti break, played exactly when the pieces are ready.
reti-opening.shortNarration: cxd5 — open lines, the Réti break

trompowsky-attack.explanation: 3.Bh4? leaves the bishop on a poor square — Black plays …d5 or …c5 to gain a free tempo against the bishop. 3.Bf4 keeps the bishop active and pressures c7/e7.
trompowsky-attack.shortNarration: Bf4 — active square, not passive Bh4

benoni-defence.explanation: In the Four Pawns Attack (f4), engine sees both moves as similar. But 7…Bg7 walks into 8.e5 (the natural pawn push) with Black's knight getting kicked from f6. 7…Nbd7 first defends the knight indirectly (after e5 dxe5 fxe5 Ng4 Nf3 the knight has the escape square e6 already controlled). Practical edge: with Nbd7 first, Black's pieces stay coordinated; with Bg7 first you face an immediate central push.

The ...b5 lever is the heart of the Benoni — but fired too early it just drops a pawn: 9...b5? 10.Bxb5 and there is no compensation, because b5 isn't yet supported. Prepare it first — 9...Re8 (then ...Na6/...Nbd7 and ...a6) — and unleash ...b5 only once it's backed up.
benoni-defence.shortNarration: Re8 first; ...b5 now just drops a pawn

benko-gambit.explanation: 4…Nxd5? loses the central knight for a pawn after 5.Nf3 with central pressure. The standard Benko 4…a6 invites White to either accept (5.bxa6) or decline (5.b6) — both lead to advantageous Black positions.

Engine sees both recaptures as similar (~13cp difference). But Bxa6 develops a piece WITH TEMPO — attacks the Bf1 directly forcing the trade Bxa6 Nxa6. With Bxa6 you reach the trade naturally; with Nxa6 the knight is offside and your bishop is still stuck behind the pawn. Practical edge: Bxa6 leaves you with active pieces and the bishop pair traded for piece coordination; Nxa6 needs three more moves to develop the bishop and never matches Bxa6's piece activity.

old-indian-defence.explanation: Engine sees both moves as similar. But 4…exd4? gives up the locked-center structure that defines the Old Indian — after 5.Nxd4 the position opens and White's pieces (with the bishop pair) outclass Black's cramped setup. 4…Nbd7 keeps the wedge intact and prepares slow positional play. Practical edge: exd4 surrenders the structural insurance Black bought with 2…d6; Nbd7 preserves it.

bird-opening.explanation: 1…e5 (From's Gambit) is sharp but theoretically dubious for Black at the top level. After 2.fxe5 d6 3.exd6 Bxd6 4.Nf3 White has a clear advantage. The principled 1…d5 challenges the center and prepares solid development.

3.g3 is engine-fine but commits Bird to a Leningrad-Dutch-reversed setup with Bg2 (kingside-fianchetto only). The mainline 3.e3 keeps the bishop options open — Bd3 (classical attacking) OR Be2 (Stonewall-style) based on Black's setup. Practical edge: 3.e3 keeps two bishop deployments available; 3.g3 commits to one structure.
1…g6 is playable but lets White fianchetto on the kingside with 2.b3 + Bb2 — Black's setup mirrors White's slow approach. The active 1…d5 is more challenging.

queens-indian.explanation: Engine sees 5…d5 as similar to 5…Be7 but pedagogically d5 cedes the e4 square permanently — after 6.cxd5 exd5 Black has a passive Carlsbad-like structure where White's b1-h7 diagonal (via Bg2) gains lasting pressure. 5…Be7 develops the bishop, keeps options for both …d5 (later) and …d6 (Hedgehog-style), and prepares castling. Practical edge: 5…Be7 keeps Black's structural choice flexible; 5…d5 locks it in passively.

budapest-gambit.explanation: 3…Ne4 (Fajarowicz) is sharp but theoretically dubious — after 4.Nf3 Nc6 5.Nbd2 the knight is forced back. The mainline 3…Ng4 immediately threatens …Nxe5 and creates more practical chances.
4…Ngxe5? trades the central knight too early — after 5.Nxe5 White's pieces dominate. The principled 4…Bc5 develops the bishop with pressure on f2, then recaptures …Nxe5 at the right moment.

kings-indian-attack.explanation: Trading with exd5 exd5 gives Black an easy, open French-style game and throws away White's plan. e5 is the whole point of the KIA — clamp the centre and launch the kingside attack.
kings-indian-attack.shortNarration: e5 — clamp the centre, then attack

kings-indian-attack.explanation: Lunging at the kingside with Nh4 is toothless against the solid ...g6 fianchetto. Stake the centre with e4 and expand on the queenside — flexibility is the KIA's strength against the KID setup.
kings-indian-attack.shortNarration: e4 — pivot to the centre vs …g6

alekhine-defence.explanation: Retreating the knight home with …Ng8 throws away the whole point of the Alekhine — Black has just lost two tempi for nothing. …Nd5 keeps the knight active in the centre, where it provokes White's pawns forward and becomes the springboard for the counterattack.
alekhine-defence.shortNarration: Nd5 — active centre, not back home

alekhine-defence.explanation: With c4 attacking the knight, …Nf4 lunges to the rim where g3 simply chases it back with tempo, costing Black even more time. …Nb6 is the sound retreat — the knight stays useful, eyeing c4 and d5, and Black continues to undermine the centre.
alekhine-defence.shortNarration: Nb6 — sound retreat, not the rim

dutch-defence.explanation: In the Leningrad, …d5 locks the position and entombs the g7-bishop behind its own pawn chain — the very piece the fianchetto exists to activate. …d6 is correct: it keeps the centre flexible and prepares the thematic …e5 break that opens the long diagonal.
dutch-defence.shortNarration: d6 — keep it flexible, free the g7-bishop

dutch-defence.explanation: Against the Staunton Gambit 2.e4, …Nf6 just drops the f-pawn to 3.exf5 with no compensation. Accept the gambit with …fxe4 — Black is a clean pawn up and, with accurate play, weathers White's development lead.
dutch-defence.shortNarration: fxe4 — accept the gambit, grab the pawn

pro-naroditsky-caro-kann.explanation: After e5 the textbook reflex everyone knows is Bf5 — get the bishop out before the chain locks. But we're playing Naroditsky's line, where c5 strikes the centre at d4 BEFORE developing the bishop. The principle: when your opponent grabs space on the flank, hit them in the centre. Bf5 just lets White play h4-h5 / g4 chasing the bishop around for the next ten moves; c5 forces White to clarify and our score with it is 64%.

After dxc5 White's grabbed the pawn and instinct says win it back — Qa5+ checks AND threatens c5. But after Nc3, the queen has to retreat empty-handed and we've burned two moves of development. The right move is e6: it unlocks our c8-bishop's diagonal (the famously locked Caro bishop), prepares Bxc5 next move with the full bishop diagonal alive, and the c5-pawn isn't actually defended yet — we'll recapture cleanly. Patience wins the pawn back AND develops a piece; the shortcut just loses time.

Reflex says Nf6 — develop the knight to its 'normal' square. Look at the board: the e5-pawn already CONTROLS f6. The knight on f6 has no good squares to go to and is just blocking our own king's view of the kingside. Nge7 is the canonical Naroditsky reroute: from e7 the knight has two beautiful jumps — f5 hitting the centre, or g6 pressuring e5 and prepping a kingside attack. The 'normal' move is the wrong one here.

After Nxf6+ in the Classical Caro-Kann, the natural …exf6? gives Black doubled f-pawns AND a passive structure. The correct move is …gxf6 — counterintuitive but correct: opens the g-file for the rook AND maintains better pawn structure (f-pawns NOT doubled). The opening of the g-file becomes Black's main attacking asset.

After …e6 in the Advance Caro-Kann, the eager Bd3? offers the bishop trade with Bxf5 — but the trade actually helps Black! Black recaptures with ...Bxd3 Qxd3 and Black's Bf5 (problem bishop) is exchanged for our active piece. The correct move is Be2 keeping the bishop pair AND continuing classical development. Don't trade bishops voluntarily in this structure.

pro-naroditsky-alapin.explanation: After Bb3 — Black's tempting d5 push (looking to challenge the e5-pawn and free pieces) actually walks into exd6 e.p.! Qxd6 O-O when White has a development lead and the bishop on b3 stares at f7. The better move is the patient e6, supporting d5 only after pieces are out.
pro-naroditsky-alapin.shortNarration: e6 — develop first, push d5 later

pro-naroditsky-alapin.explanation: After …Nf6 in the d5-open line — the natural Nf3 is fine, but Naroditsky's signature is Na3! heading to b5 for the queen-fork outpost. Nf3 develops too modestly; Na3 wins concrete tempi on the c7 prize square. His 13% pick at this position scores 71.3% vs 66% for routine Nf3.

After d4 in the d6-mainline — Black's natural cxd4 just helps White (open c-file, central pawn duo). The principled move is Nf6 first, forcing White to declare the centre. After Nf6 White plays e5 kicking the knight or Nc3 developing; either way Black's structure is more flexible than after the trade.

In a transposition where Black's knight on f6 reaches a position with the d5-pawn — taking with Nxd5 puts the knight on the WRONG square (vulnerable to Bc4) when cxd4 keeps the structure flexible. The data shows Nxd5 leads to the Alapin's signature crushing positions; cxd4 keeps Black in the game.

After …d6 in the Alapin, the over-cautious Nf3? wastes the supported d4 push — Black has committed without ...Nf6 or ...d5, so White CAN play d4 immediately and reach the dream Alapin structure. The correct move is d4! claiming the centre. After ...d6, the d4 push is justified (unlike after ...Nc6 where d4 is premature).

pro-naroditsky-kid.explanation: After Be2 the natural move is …e5! striking the centre immediately — the move that defines the KID. Playing …Nbd7 first delays the central strike and lets White complete development with Be3 + O-O, blunting our middlegame plans. The Mar del Plata mainline starts with e5 right now.

After e4 in the Fianchetto, taking with …exd4 prematurely opens the position favouring White's Bg2 on the long diagonal. The correct move is …c6 supporting d5 and preparing the queenside expansion plan with ...Qa5 + ...b5. Wait for White to commit before opening lines.

After Be3 in the Sämisch, the tempting …c5? prematurely commits the c-pawn before the Bronstein/Panno queenside setup is ready. White answers dxc5 dxc5 Qxd8 Rxd8 Nb5 hitting c7 with annoying tactics. The correct move is …a6 preparing ...b5 in the canonical Panno move order — let the c5 push come AFTER ...b5 secures the queenside.

After …e5 in the Classical, the careless dxe5? hands Black the perfect game: …dxe5 Qxd8 Rxd8 — Black has an open d-file, the bishop pair, and a knight outpost on d4 coming. The correct move is O-O keeping tension and letting Black declare. The Mar del Plata mainline runs through O-O exd4 Nxd4 Re8 — NOT through an early central trade by White.
pro-naroditsky-kid.shortNarration: White: O-O keep tension, not dxe5

pro-naroditsky-kid.explanation: After Rd1 in the Sämisch, the natural-looking …cxd4? simplifies prematurely — White recaptures with the knight and the trade-down sequence favours White's developed pieces. The correct move is …b5! continuing the Bronstein/Panno queenside push BEFORE simplifying. The b5 hits c4 and opens lines while Black still has full development tempo.

pro-naroditsky-kia.explanation: After e4 the natural-looking …Nc6? actually blocks the c-pawn AND commits the knight to a less flexible square. The correct move is …Nbd7 keeping the c-pawn free for ...c6 + ...c5 expansion plans. The Nbd7 also reroutes to Nf8-Ne6 in some structures, giving Black more flexibility.

After e4 in the KIA vs ...d5 setup, Black's tempting …dxe4? opens the position too soon for White's developed pieces. After dxe4 White has the Bg2 dominating the long diagonal, the half-open d-file, and active piece play — Black has no compensation. The correct move is …O-O completing development before any structural decision, letting White be the one to commit.

After e4 in the symmetric KIA, the over-aggressive …c5? weakens the d5-square AND gives White's Nbd2 the perfect outpost via Nc4. The correct move is …Nc6 developing classically and preparing ...Re8 + queenside expansion. The KIA symmetric structure rewards patience — Black's c-pawn should support, not race.

After …O-O the over-eager Nc4? puts the knight on a square where Black can kick it with ...b5 (gaining tempo) AND the knight on c4 doesn't have great follow-ups since Black hasn't committed any pieces yet. The correct move is Re1 supporting e4 first, then deciding whether Nc4 or Nh4 is the right reroute based on Black's setup.

After …e5 in the KIA vs Pirc, the careless dxe5? trades the centre too early and hands Black the open e-file plus equality. The correct move is Nc3 supporting the centre and keeping tension. The d4-pawn is fine where it is — let Black be the one to commit the exchange.

pro-naroditsky-najdorf.explanation: After Qf3 in the English Attack with Bg5, Black's natural-looking ...O-O? lets White play O-O-O + g4-g5 with a coming kingside crash. The correct move is …Qc7 loading the c-file AND preparing the …b5 push. The queen on c7 has multiple roles: defends, attacks, and stays flexible.

After Bg5 (the English Attack via Bg5), the natural-looking …Nbd7? blocks the queen's diagonal AND lets White play Bxf6 doubling Black's pawns without consequence. The correct move is …e6 preparing ...Be7 to break the pin AND keeping the queenside flexible for the ...b5 race. The Najdorf's mainline plan needs ...e6 first.

After Nb3 in the English Attack, the over-aggressive …d5? challenges the centre but opens lines for White's pieces: exd5 Nxd5 Nxd5 Qxd5 and White's pieces are MORE coordinated than Black's. The correct move is …Be6 completing development with the bishop on its natural square — supports d5 indirectly AND prepares ...Nbd7 + ...b5 in the canonical race.

After f4 in the English Attack with Bg5, the natural …Nbd7? blocks the queen's d-file AND lets White play Bxf6 doubling Black's pawns without compensation. The correct move is …Be7 breaking the pin first AND completing kingside development. The Nbd7 reroute comes after the pin is broken.

After Be3 in the Classical, the tempting …Ng4? attacks the bishop but White just retreats Bg5 and Black has wasted tempi. The correct move is …O-O completing development first — the position is positional, not tactical, and knight excursions just lose tempo.

pro-naroditsky-rossolimo.explanation: After Bb5+ Black's …Nbd7 blockade is passive — the knight on d7 is awkward, blocking the bishop's development AND limiting later …c5 push ideas. The cleanest response is …Bd7 offering the immediate trade. Bxd7+ Qxd7 simplifies and Black gets a comfortable game without the bishop pair handicap.

After exd5 in the Rossolimo proper, the wrong recapture …exd5? leaves Black with an isolated d-pawn AND a passive setup — the e-file becomes White's open road. The correct recapture is …Nxd5 keeping the pawn structure intact and the e-file half-open for Black. The recapture choice IS the variation — get it wrong and the whole Rossolimo middlegame favours White.

After O-O with the Nd7 blockade setup, the careless …a6? attacks the bishop too early — the bishop just retreats to Bd3 and we've wasted a tempo. The correct move is …Ngf6 completing development first; the bishop retreat will come naturally later (and the …a6 push can wait until it's actually useful, like preparing ...b5).

After O-O in the Rossolimo vs ...g6, the tempting e5? grabs space but Black answers ...Nh6-Nf5 reaching active piece play AND the e5-pawn is loose. The correct move is Re1 supporting e4 AND preparing classical development. The space gain has to come slowly in the Rossolimo, not by force.

pro-naroditsky-alekhine.explanation: After d4 the natural-looking …Nb6 retreats too early — White answers c4 chasing the knight to a4 with serious cramping. The correct move is …d6 hitting the e5 pawn and forcing White to declare. After exd6 we recapture; after Nf3 we get classical Modern Alekhine development.

After Nf3, the immediate …dxe5? grabs the wedge pawn but loses the knight's outpost: Nxe5 with active piece play for White and our knight on d5 is loose. The correct move is …Nb6 — preventive retreat that prevents c4 chases AND prepares ...Bf5 + ...Nc6 classical development. The Modern Alekhine runs through ...Nb6, not early ...dxe5.

After …Nc6 in the c4 Modern Main, White's tempting d5? kicks the knight but leaves the d6-pawn weak AND the e-file fully open for Black's rook. The correct move is Be2 completing development and supporting the IQP structure. The d4-pawn is fine where it is; trying to chase Black's pieces with a premature push just gives Black free tempo.

After O-O the wrong-bishop development …Bg4? exposes the bishop to h3 ideas AND doesn't address Black's central setup. The correct move is …Nd7 challenging the centralised White knight on e5 AND preparing classical development. The Bf5 stays put.

After …d6 in the Two Knights Alekhine, the natural-looking Bg5? pins the f6-knight but Black just plays ...h6 and the position is unclear. The correct move is Bxc6 trading immediately — the resulting Spanish-style pawn structure favours White's space advantage AND the bishop pair will compensate Black's doubled c-pawns insufficiently.

pro-naroditsky-ruy-lopez.explanation: After c3 in the Closed Spanish, Black's …Bc5? exposes the bishop to White's d4 push winning a tempo. The correct move is …d6 supporting e5 AND preparing the standard Ruy maneuvering ...Na5-Nc4 or …Nb8-Nbd7. Don't volunteer the bishop to be kicked.

After O-O, Black's …Nxe4? grabs the pawn but walks into the Open Ruy where White has the Tarrasch Trap and other tactics. Unless you've memorised 30 moves of Open Ruy theory, the safe move is …Be7 entering the Closed Spanish where Black has time to develop solidly before the centre opens.

After d4 in the Berlin Defense, the natural …exd4? loses material to Re1 pinning the e4-knight (the Tarrasch Trap setup). The correct move is …Nd6 retreating the knight AND triggering the Berlin Endgame transition. The …exd4 grab is a classic Berlin trap — don't fall for it.

After …O-O the immediate d4? opens the position before White's setup is complete — Black answers ...exd4 cxd4 ...Bg4 with tactical pressure. The correct move is h3 preventing ...Bg4 AND preparing the future d4 push at the right moment. Patience: the Ruy is a slow strangulation.

After …Nf6 in the Steinitz Defense Deferred, the developing Re1 is fine but the active d5! gains queenside space AND locks the centre favourably. The Re1 move is slow; d5 is the principled aggressive choice in this specific structure.

pro-naroditsky-jobava-london.explanation: After Bf4 in the Jobava, Black's careless …Nbd7? walks into Nb5! threatening Nc7+ winning material. The correct move is …c5 challenging the centre AND denying the Nb5 square. The Bf4 setup is positional but contains tactics; ignore them and you lose.

After …Bd6 offering the trade, the cautious Bg3? keeps the bishop but locks it out of the kingside attack. The correct move is Bxd6 accepting — the doubled d-pawns Black gets AND the half-open c-file for our rook AND the kingside attack with Bd3 + Qe2 + Ne5 all favour White. Trading is the whole point of the Bf4 setup; declining wastes the system's main asset.

After Bd3, the immediate …Bxd3? simplifies prematurely — Black trades his most active piece (the Bf5) for White's developing bishop, AND White's Qxd3 lands centrally with a kingside attack on h7. The correct move is …Be7 completing development first; the bishop trade can wait until Black is ready for the resulting position with proper king safety.

After Bd3 the over-eager …cxd4? opens the position too early — White recaptures with the knight (Nxd4) and develops with a clear tempo edge. The correct move is …h6 preventing future Bg5 pins AND preparing ...Bd6 development. Patience in the Jobava; Black has to develop before opening lines.

After Nf3 the over-active …Qb6? attacks b2 but White just plays Qb1 (or Nd2 defending) and Black's queen is exposed AND undeveloped. The correct move is …e6 completing classical development first. The queen excursions come later, after pieces are out.

pro-naroditsky-fantasy-caro.explanation: After f3 the principled reply is ...dxe4 fxe4 e5 — Black trades pawns AND breaks centrally. The premature ...e5 (without taking on e4 first) lets White play exd5 cxd5 dxe5 winning a clean pawn AND keeping a structural edge. Always trade on e4 before playing ...e5.

After fxe4 the correct break is ...e5 IMMEDIATELY to challenge White's strong central pawn duo. The natural ...Nf6 develops a piece but lets White play e5! locking up the centre AND gaining a permanent space advantage. The Nf6-Nfd7 retreat then drops the bishop. Always play ...e5 first.

After Nf3 the pin attempt ...Bg4 is premature — White plays dxe5 trading AND if …Bxf3 Qxf3 Qxd1+ Kxd1 Black has given up the bishop pair for nothing. The correct move is ...Bd6 supporting the e5-pawn AND preparing castling. The Italian-style setup with ...Bd6 is the main line.

After Bc4 the natural-looking pin ...Bg4 runs into Bxf7+ Kxf7 Ng5+ — discovered attack winning the bishop on g4 AND material. The correct development is ...Nf6 challenging White's e4-pawn AND supporting kingside structure. Always complete development before pinning.

pro-gothamchess-caro-kann.explanation: This is the cardinal Caro-Kann error and the very thing the opening exists to avoid. Playing …e6 here buries the light-squared bishop behind its own pawn chain — turning the Caro into a bad French. The whole point of …c6 (instead of …e6) is that the bishop comes OUT to f5 or g4 FIRST, and only then does …e6 support the centre. Develop the bishop, then close the centre.
pro-gothamchess-caro-kann.shortNarration: Bf5 first — never bury the bishop

pro-gothamchess-caro-kann.explanation: Dropping the bishop back to g4 to trade it for the f3-knight throws away Black's best piece. In the Advance, the light-squared bishop — already developed outside the chain on f5 — is the pride of the whole Caro setup. Trading it concedes the bishop pair and leaves Black passive on the light squares. Instead, complete the plan: …Ne7 (heading for g6 or f5) keeps every piece working. Treasure that bishop; don't volunteer it.

Lunging with …d4 to kick the c3-knight throws away Black's central tension far too early. The pawn on d4 becomes overextended — White rerouts with Ne2 and later c3 to undermine it, and Black has nothing behind it. Against the Réti/KIA move-order, the right plan is to finish development: …Bg4 pins the f3-knight, then …e6 and …Nbd7 build the solid Caro structure. Don't chase pieces with pawns before you're developed.
pro-gothamchess-caro-kann.shortNarration: Develop with Bg4 — don’t lunge d4

pro-gothamchess-caro-kann.explanation: Playing …Nf6 immediately invites Nxf6+, and after …exf6 (or …gxf6) Black accepts a damaged pawn structure with no compensation prepared. In the Classical, move-order matters: …Bf5 FIRST develops the bishop outside the chain, hits the e4-knight, and only THEN does Black sort out the knights. The …Nf6 / doubled-f-pawn structure can be a deliberate weapon (a wall that controls e5), but as a reflex it just concedes structure — …Bf5 is the cleaner, more flexible route.
pro-gothamchess-caro-kann.shortNarration: Bf5 first — hit the knight, develop

pro-gothamchess-trompowsky.explanation: When Black hits the bishop with …Ne4, the timid Bh4 lets Black off the hook — after …g5 the bishop is awkward and Black equalises comfortably. The principled Trompowsky answer is the aggressive h4! — supporting the bishop on g5 AND opening the rook's file for an attack. If Black grabs with …Nxg5, hxg5 opens the h-file straight at the king. Meet the knight hit with a punch, not a retreat.

Trading on f6 immediately against …d5 is premature — after …exf6 (or …gxf6) Black gets the bishop pair and a solid centre for free, and White has given up the tension with nothing to show for it. The patient e3 keeps options open: build with c3 and Nd2, pressure the queenside with Qb3, and only take on f6 when it damages Black's structure. Don't trade your good bishop without a reason.
pro-gothamchess-trompowsky.shortNarration: e3 — keep the tension, don’t trade early

pro-gothamchess-trompowsky.explanation: When Black plays …Qb6 hitting b2, the passive b3 wastes a tempo and blunts White's own queenside. The Trompowsky idea is to GAMBIT the b2-pawn: Nc3 develops, and after …Qxb2 White gets a huge lead in development with Bd2, e4, and f4 building a big centre while the black queen gets chased around. The pawn is a small price for a raging initiative. Develop and let Black grab the poison.

After doubling Black's f-pawns with Bxf6 exf6, lunging e4 gives Black exactly the central break and piece play he wants — the doubled pawns become dynamic. The cleaner plan is c4, claiming queenside space and clamping the d5-square so Black's structure stays static. Combined with g3, Bg2, and Ne2, White presses the long-term weakness of the doubled f-pawns. Keep Black's structure frozen, don't help it become active.
pro-gothamchess-trompowsky.shortNarration: c4 — clamp d5, keep pawns frozen

pro-gothamchess-english.explanation: In the Reversed Sicilian, Nf3 invites …e4! kicking the knight and handing Black easy space — a reversed-Sicilian tempo trick. The cleaner move is g3, preparing Bg2 to fianchetto and hit the e5-pawn and the long diagonal first. Develop the kingside bishop before the knight commits, and Black never gets the …e4 lunge for free. Move order matters in the English.

Against the Symmetric …c5, the timid e4 lets Black equalise comfortably with a normal setup. The principled strike is d4! — challenging the centre at once. After …cxd4 Nxd4, White reaches a Maroczy-style bind with the c4-pawn clamping d5 and a clear space edge. Don't drift in the Symmetric; the d4 break is what gives White the pull.
pro-gothamchess-english.shortNarration: d4 — strike for the Maroczy bind

pro-gothamchess-english.explanation: When Black sets up the Stonewall with …f5, the routine d4 lets Black get the structure he wants — a solid, blocked position. The aggressive answer is g4! — striking at the f5-pawn before Black is ready. It rips open the kingside, exposes Black's weakened light squares, and gives White a dangerous initiative. Against the Stonewall, undermine the f5-pawn, don't play into the block.

In the Botvinnik System, the immediate fxe5 dxe5 d5 is one valid path, but the cleaner Botvinnik handling is Nf3 first — developing, defending d4, and keeping the central tension on White's terms. Premature captures release the tension before White is fully developed. Build the c4/d4/e4/f4 wall, get the pieces out, and only then resolve the centre and storm. Patience powers the avalanche.
pro-gothamchess-english.shortNarration: Nf3 — develop before resolving the centre

pro-gothamchess-vienna.explanation: The whole point of the Vienna against …Nf6 is the gambit f4! — striking at the e5-pawn and opening the f-file for a kingside attack. The quiet g3 fianchetto is playable but throws away the Vienna's sting and lets Black equalise easily. When Black allows it, play the gambit: f4 is the move that makes the Vienna dangerous.

After the central clash with …d5, the principled capture is fxe5! — hitting the f6-knight and keeping the f-file open for the attack. The natural-looking exd5 instead opens the centre for Black's pieces and surrenders the whole point of the gambit. Take toward the centre with the f-pawn, chase the knight, and keep the initiative.
pro-gothamchess-vienna.shortNarration: fxe5 — chase the knight, keep the f-file

pro-gothamchess-vienna.explanation: When Black grabs on e4, the strong move is Qf3! — double-attacking the e4-knight and the f7-square, forcing favourable simplification. Recapturing immediately with Nxe4 lets Black play …dxe4 hitting nothing and equalising the structure. The Qf3 zwischenzug is the engine-approved heart of the Vienna Gambit main line — pressure first, recapture later.

When Black accepts the gambit with …exf4, the most testing reply is e5! — kicking the f6-knight back to g8 and grabbing a big space advantage while Black is undeveloped. The quiet Bc4 lets Black consolidate the extra pawn with …d5. Stake the centre at once: e5 cramps Black and gives White the lead in development that justifies the gambit.
pro-gothamchess-vienna.shortNarration: e5 — kick the knight, grab space

pro-gothamchess-italian.explanation: After c3 preparing the centre, the whole point is to follow with d4! — striking in the centre while Black's pieces are committed. The timid d3 wastes the c3-tempo and lets Black equalise comfortably with …d6 and …a6. When you've played c3, commit to d4: that's the Giuoco Piano's central break and the reason c3 was played.
pro-gothamchess-italian.shortNarration: d4 — the central break c3 prepared

pro-gothamchess-italian.explanation: Black's greedy …Nxd5?? walks into the famous Fried Liver Attack: Nxf7! sacrifices the knight to drag the king out into the open after …Kxf7 Qf3+, where White's attack is overwhelming in practice. The timid Nf3 retreat throws the whole point away and lets Black consolidate the extra piece. When Black recaptures on d5, know the Fried Liver cold — Nxf7 is the punishment.

In the Evans Gambit after …Bxb4, the point is c3! — gaining a tempo on the bishop and preparing d4 to build the big centre. The greedy Nxe5 wins a pawn back immediately but throws away the entire gambit idea: after …Nxe5 Black is fine. The Evans is about development and the centre, not regaining the pawn. Play c3 and d4, and let the initiative do the work.

After castling, White faces the key choice. The open d4! is his most testing try — striking the centre while Black's pieces are committed. After …Bxd4 Nxd4 Nxd4, White plays Bg5 pinning the f6-knight and f4 storming the kingside, exactly the attacking plan from his games. The passive Re1 just shuffles a rook and lets Black equalise with …d6 and …a6. Commit to d4 and the Bg5/f4 attack.

pro-gothamchess-london.explanation: When Black hits b2 with …Qb6, the passive b3 weakens the queenside and blunts White's own play. The principled answer is Nc3! — developing and offering the b2-pawn as a gambit: after …Qxb2 Nb5! traps the queen ideas and gives White a huge lead in development. Don't cower with b3; develop and let Black grab the poison if he dares.

In the Jobava London, the point is the Nb5! raid — hitting the weak c7-square and provoking concessions like …Na6 and an awkward king move. The routine Nf3 throws away the whole idea and transposes to a tame position. When Black plays …e6 in the Jobava, jump the knight into b5 and harass: that's what makes this London hybrid dangerous.
pro-gothamchess-london.shortNarration: Nb5 — the c7-raid, not quiet Nf3

pro-gothamchess-london.explanation: It's tempting to grab the centre with e4, but here it simply drops a pawn: …dxe4 and White has no easy way to regain it. The whole point of the London is the modest e3 — supporting the d4-pawn and the Bf4, building the solid pyramid behind which White develops harmoniously. Resist the e4 lunge; the London is a system of small, solid moves, not a centre grab.

Against the …g6 fianchetto, the most testing try is h4! — launching the opposite-side-castling storm before Black is ready. The routine Nf3 commits to a quiet game and lets Black equalise comfortably with …O-O and …c5. When Black fianchettoes, consider the h4-h5 pawn storm: it's the London's most dangerous weapon against the King's Indian setup.

pro-gothamchess-ponziani.explanation: The whole idea of c3 is to support d4! — striking the centre immediately. The timid d3 wastes the c3-move and leaves White with a passive Italian-like position a tempo down. After d4 exd4 e5, White chases the f6-knight and grabs the centre. Commit to d4: that's the Ponziani's reason for being.
pro-gothamchess-ponziani.shortNarration: d4 — the central strike c3 prepared

pro-gothamchess-ponziani.explanation: Against the principled …d5, the routine exd5 Qxd5 just gives Black an easy game with the centralised queen. The critical try is Qa4! — pinning the c6-knight to the e5-pawn, the move that fights for an advantage. After …f6 or …Bd7, White follows with Bb5 and d4 to exploit the pin. Don't trade tamely; the Qa4 pin is the Ponziani's main weapon against …d5.
pro-gothamchess-ponziani.shortNarration: Qa4 — pin the knight, fight for an edge

pro-gothamchess-ponziani.explanation: Here White has just played e5, chasing the f6-knight before recapturing on d4. The move order matters: by inserting e5 first, White gains a tempo on the knight and keeps the option of Qb3 hitting the loose d5-knight. Rushing cxd4 immediately lets Black equalise. Chase with e5, provoke …Nd5, then Qb3 — the tempo-gaining sequence is the point.
pro-gothamchess-ponziani.shortNarration: e5 — chase the knight before recapturing

pro-gothamchess-anti-sicilian.explanation: The whole point of the Anti-Sicilian is to sidestep the deeply-theoretical Open Sicilian. d4 enters the main lines where Black is well-prepared. The Rossolimo Bb5! pins toward c6 and steers the game into structural channels Black knows less well — White trades Bxc6 to double the pawns and plays a positional game. Pick the Anti-Sicilian: that's the repertoire's whole idea.

Against the …g6 fianchetto, the principled move is Bxc6! — trading immediately to saddle Black with doubled c-pawns before he can play …a6 and …b5 to harass the bishop. Retreating with Bc4 lets Black off the hook and the bishop becomes a target. Cash in the structural concession with Bxc6, then play c3 and d4 against the doubled pawns.

After Bxc6 and d3, when Black plays …d5, the ambitious e5! grabs a central space wedge and cramps Black, the Carlsen-style accelerated plan. The routine exd5 just opens the position for Black's bishop pair and relieves the cramped position. Ram e5 to keep Black passive behind the doubled pawns and build a kingside initiative.
pro-gothamchess-anti-sicilian.shortNarration: e5 — the space wedge, keep Black cramped

pro-gothamchess-milner-barry.explanation: When Black hits d4 with …Qb6, the Milner-Barry idea is Bd3! — offering the d4-pawn as a gambit. After …cxd4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nxd4 Qxd4, White gets a huge lead in development and a kingside attack for the pawn. The passive a3 or Be2 defends tamely and surrenders the initiative. Play the gambit: Bd3 is the move that makes the Milner-Barry dangerous.

After Black grabs the gambit pawn with …Qxd4, the point is rapid development: Nc3! brings a piece out with tempo, eyeing d5 and b5, and prepares Qe2, Kh1, and the f-pawn storm. Chasing with Qa4+ to win the pawn back lets Black consolidate and defeats the gambit's purpose. Develop and attack — the lead in development IS the compensation, not the pawn.
pro-gothamchess-milner-barry.shortNarration: Nc3 — develop fast, don’t chase the pawn

pro-gothamchess-milner-barry.explanation: When Black reroutes the knight to f5 attacking d4, the principled move is Bxf5! — trading to saddle Black with a doubled, weak f5-pawn after …exf5. The casual O-O lets Black keep a strong knight on f5 blockading the position. Cash in the structural damage: Bxf5 gives White a permanent target on f5 and the better long-term game.

pro-gothamchess-fantasy-caro.explanation: The whole point of f3 is to recapture with fxe4! — building a broad e4/d4 pawn centre, the Fantasy's entire idea. Developing with Bc4 first lets Black hold onto the extra e4-pawn with …exf3 or …f5, throwing away the centre that justifies the slightly weakening f3. Take with the f-pawn immediately: the imposing centre and the open f-file are the compensation for the committal third move.

When Black plays …Qb6 eyeing b2 against the …g6 line, the principled move is Qd2! — calmly developing and DARING Black to grab the poison pawn. After …Qxb2 Rb1 chases the queen to a3, and White has a huge lead in development for the pawn. The passive Rb1 immediately just defends and surrenders the initiative. Offer b2 with Qd2 and play the gambit.
pro-gothamchess-fantasy-caro.shortNarration: Qd2 — offer the b2 poison pawn

pro-gothamchess-fantasy-caro.explanation: When Black pins with …Bb4 in the …e6 line, the active a3! questions the bishop immediately. After …Bxc3+ bxc3, White gets the bishop pair and a powerful pawn centre with attacking chances on the kingside (the Qg4-Qxg7 raid). The passive Bd2 lets Black keep the tension and equalise comfortably. Challenge the pin with a3 and take the bishop pair.
pro-gothamchess-fantasy-caro.shortNarration: a3 — question the pin, win the pair

pro-gothamchess-stafford-refute.explanation: Here is the heart of the Stafford. The safe refutation is d3! — opening the bishop and preparing Be2 to trade off Black's attackers, keeping the extra pawn with no risk. The natural-looking Nc3 walks into the famous trap …Bg4! and …Nd4 with a vicious attack on f3 and the king. Against the Stafford, play d3 and develop calmly — never grab more or develop carelessly into the gambit's tricks.

After …Bc5, the careful move is Be2! — preparing to meet …Ng4 by simply trading the knight. The natural h3 (stopping …Ng4) actually walks into …Nxe4! dxe4 Bxf2+ winning the queen with a discovered attack, a classic Stafford trap. Don't weaken the kingside with h3 — develop with Be2 and let Black's attack hit a brick wall.
pro-gothamchess-stafford-refute.shortNarration: Be2 — develop safely, avoid the trap

pro-gothamchess-stafford-refute.explanation: In the ambitious e5 line, after …Ne4 the strong move is d4! — building the big pawn centre and keeping the extra pawn with a space advantage. The timid d3 kicks the knight but gives up the chance to clamp the centre, letting Black free his position. When you've committed to e5, follow with d4 to build a dominating centre against the Stafford.

pro-gothamchess-caro-advance-white.explanation: Against …Bf5, his signature is the aggressive h4! — gaining kingside space and threatening h5 to harass the bishop. The routine Nf3 allows Black the comfortable …e6 and …Ne7 setup with an easy game. The h4-thrust is what makes the modern Advance dangerous: it grabs space, restricts the light bishop, and sets up the Bg5 pin. Play h4 and seize the initiative.
pro-gothamchess-caro-advance-white.shortNarration: h4 — grab space, harass the bishop

pro-gothamchess-caro-advance-white.explanation: When Black plays …h6 to prevent Bg5, the maximalist g4! grabs huge kingside space and chases the f5-bishop. The timid Nf3 gives up the chance to bind Black. After g4, the bishop must retreat passively, and White follows with c4 and h5 to dominate both wings. Against …h6, the g4 space-grab is the most testing — don't shy away from it.
pro-gothamchess-caro-advance-white.shortNarration: g4 — grab space, chase the bishop

pro-gothamchess-caro-advance-white.explanation: Against the …c5 break, the ambitious dxc5! grabs the pawn and forces Black to spend time regaining it, giving White a lead in development and the e5-wedge. The passive c3 just defends d4 and lets Black equalise with a comfortable French-style structure. Take the pawn with dxc5 and develop quickly — the extra tempo and the cramping e5-pawn are the point.
pro-gothamchess-caro-advance-white.shortNarration: dxc5 — grab the pawn, develop fast

pro-gothamchess-kia.explanation: The whole point of the King's Indian Attack is the e4 break! — striking the centre and preparing the e5 wedge and the kingside attack. The passive c3 drifts without a plan and lets Black seize the initiative with …d4 or queenside expansion. When your pieces are set (Nf3, g3, Bg2, d3, Nbd2), play e4 and follow with e5 and the Nf1-h2-g4 reroute. The KIA is an attacking system — commit to e4.

When Black expands with …b5 against the KIA, the key is e5! — grabbing the kingside space wedge that defines the King's Indian Attack and starting the attack. Reacting on the queenside with a4 plays into Black's hands, where he is faster. Ignore the queenside and play on YOUR side: e5 cramps Black, the knight reroutes Nf1-h2-g4, and White's attack on the king outruns Black's counterplay.

Against the …c5/…g6 Sicilian setup, the KIA way is the modest d3! — keeping the centre closed for the slow kingside attack with e4, Re1, and Nf1-h2-g4. Lunging d4 opens the centre and transposes into an Open-Sicilian-like position where Black is comfortable. Stay true to the King's Indian Attack: play d3, build the kingside, and attack the king behind the closed centre.
pro-gothamchess-kia.shortNarration: d3 — keep it closed for the KIA

pro-gothamchess-closed-sicilian.explanation: His signature anti-Sicilian is the early Qxd4! — recapturing with the queen to reach an Open-Sicilian-like position a tempo up, then castling queenside for a kingside attack. Recapturing with Nf3 transposes into normal Open Sicilian theory where Black is well-prepared. The Qxd4 approach sidesteps theory: the queen sits actively, Nc3 is already developed, and White heads for the O-O-O attack.
pro-gothamchess-closed-sicilian.shortNarration: Qxd4 — the early queen, sidestep theory

pro-gothamchess-closed-sicilian.explanation: After …Nc6 hits the queen, the move is Qd2! — keeping the queen active and connecting it to the kingside attack and the long diagonal. Retreating all the way to d1 wastes the tempo gained and undoes the whole point of the early Qxd4. The queen belongs on d2, supporting b3-Bb2, f4, and the O-O-O opposite-castling storm. Keep the queen active.

With the b3-Bb2 setup complete, the thematic move is O-O-O! — castling queenside to commit to the kingside pawn storm with f3 and g4-h4. Developing the knight to f3 instead blocks the f-pawn that White needs for the f3/g4 storm and delays the whole attacking plan (the knight belongs on e2, not f3). The Closed/Nc3 Sicilian with Qd2 is built for opposite-side castling: O-O-O first, then storm Black's king while yours stays safe behind the Bb2.

pro-gothamchess-scandinavian.explanation: After Nc3 attacks the queen, the best square is …Qa5! — pinning nothing but staying active, eyeing a5-e1 and supporting a quick …Bf5, …c6, and queenside development. The greedy …Qe5+ invites Be2 and rapid development with tempo against the exposed queen, while …Qd8 is too passive. The Scandinavian's main line runs through …Qa5 — the queen is safe and useful there.
pro-gothamchess-scandinavian.shortNarration: Qa5 — the safe, active queen square

pro-gothamchess-scandinavian.explanation: In the modern …Nf6 Scandinavian, after f3 questions the bishop, the principled move is …Bf5! — keeping the bishop on its strong diagonal and preparing …e6 and …Bxc2 ideas or …Nxd5 recapture. Grabbing with …Bxf3 hands White the bishop pair and a strong centre for nothing. Retreat the bishop to f5 and keep the Scandinavian's piece activity.

When White grabs space with c4 to hold the extra d5-pawn, the strong gambit try is …e6! — striking at the d5-pawn immediately and opening lines for rapid development and a lead in initiative. The routine …Nxd5 isn't possible (the pawn is defended by c4), and passive play lets White consolidate the extra pawn. Hit the centre with …e6 and play the Icelandic-Palme gambit for activity.
pro-gothamchess-scandinavian.shortNarration: e6 — strike the centre, gambit for activity

pro-gothamchess-qgd.explanation: In the QGD, the whole point is to keep the centre solid: …Be7! breaks the pin and prepares …O-O and …h6 with a rock-solid structure. Grabbing the pawn with …dxc4 surrenders the centre and invites e4 with a big space advantage for White — that's the Queen's Gambit Accepted, a different opening. The QGD keeps the …d5/…e6 chain intact: develop with …Be7 and stay solid.
pro-gothamchess-qgd.shortNarration: Be7 — keep the QGD solid, hold d5

pro-gothamchess-qgd.explanation: In the Carlsbad/Exchange structure, Black's freeing plan is …Re8 followed by the …Nbd7-f8-g6 reroute and the …e5 break — the classic antidote to White's minority attack. Playing …b6 weakens the queenside light squares (c6) right where White wants to attack with b4-b5. Don't help the minority attack: play …Re8, reroute the knight, and prepare …e5 to free the position.

In the Nimzo-QGD with Qc2, his choice is …d5! — striking the centre and transposing into a favourable QGD structure where the …Bb4 pin and the …d5 chain give Black a comfortable game. The passive …Nc6 blocks the c-pawn and lets White expand with a3 and e4 unchallenged. Strike the centre with …d5 and reach the solid QGD/Nimzo structure he wins with.
pro-gothamchess-qgd.shortNarration: d5 — strike the centre, reach the QGD

pro-gothamchess-french-defense.explanation: His signature Rubinstein recapture is …gxf6! — accepting doubled f-pawns in exchange for the bishop pair, the open g-file, and a dynamic, aggressive position with …e5 and …O-O-O to follow. The natural …Qxf6 keeps the structure clean but leads to a passive, equal position with no winning chances. The …gxf6 structure is what makes his French a fighting weapon — take with the g-pawn and play for the attack.

Against the Advance e5, the principled break is …c5! — striking immediately at the base of White's pawn chain (the d4-pawn) to generate queenside counterplay with …Qb6 and …cxd4. Developing passively with …Ne7 first lets White consolidate the big space advantage and play a comfortable game. Hit the chain at its base with …c5 — that's the time-tested French Advance antidote.
pro-gothamchess-french-defense.shortNarration: c5 — strike the pawn chain base

pro-gothamchess-french-defense.explanation: In the Exchange French, the way to fight for a win is active development: …Bd6! aims the bishop at h2, prepares …Bg4 to pin, and sets up a kingside attack or opposite-side castling. Routine symmetrical development with …Nf6 first invites a dead-equal, drawish game. Refuse the draw: develop the bishop actively to d6, pin with …Bg4, and create imbalance from the supposedly equal Exchange French.
pro-gothamchess-french-defense.shortNarration: Bd6 — active development, refuse the draw

pro-gothamchess-pirc-defense.explanation: Against the aggressive Austrian Attack, the principled counter is …c5! — striking the centre immediately before White completes the kingside build-up. Castling passively with …O-O invites White's e5 and a crushing kingside pawn storm (f4-f5) against the king. Hit the centre first with …c5: it challenges d4, opens lines for counterplay, and stops White from getting a free attack. Counterattack, don't sit and defend.
pro-gothamchess-pirc-defense.shortNarration: c5 — counter the centre, not passive O-O

pro-gothamchess-pirc-defense.explanation: Against the 150 Attack (Be3 + f3 + Qd2 + O-O-O aiming for a kingside mate), castling kingside with …O-O walks straight into White's attack with h4-h5 and the Bh6 trade. The right plan is the immediate …b5! — striking out on the queenside, preparing …b4 to counterattack White's king on the queenside, where White intends to castle. In these opposite-side races, strike first on the queenside with …b5 and …b4 — don't castle into the storm.
pro-gothamchess-pirc-defense.shortNarration: b5 — counter on the queenside, not O-O

pro-gothamchess-pirc-defense.explanation: The Pirc's whole idea is the kingside fianchetto: …g6! preparing …Bg7 to train the bishop on the long diagonal and pressure White's centre from afar. The premature …e5 opens the centre while Black is underdeveloped — after dxe5 dxe5 Qxd8+ Kxd8 Black loses castling rights for nothing. Stay true to the Pirc setup: …g6, …Bg7, …O-O, and counterattack the centre with …c5 or …e5 only when ready.

two-knights-defence.explanation: Recapturing with 5...Nxd5 walks straight into the Fried Liver: 6.Nxf7! Kxf7 7.Qf3+ drags the king out with a raging attack for the piece. The cool antidote is 5...Na5, hitting the c4-bishop — Black returns the pawn at leisure and reaches a sound, slightly better structure.
two-knights-defence.shortNarration: Na5 hits the bishop, dodges the Fried Liver

philidor-defence.explanation: The pin 3...Bg4 is an illusion: 4.Nxe5! refutes it — after 4...dxe5 5.Qxg4 White nets a clean pawn, because capturing the knight opened the d1-queen's line straight to the loose g4-bishop. Develop calmly with 3...Be7 and keep the pieces coordinated.
philidor-defence.shortNarration: Be7 develops; the Bg4 pin drops a pawn

albin-countergambit.explanation: The d4-pawn IS the Albin — the cramping wedge is Black's whole compensation for the gambit pawn. Developing 4...Bf5 abandons it: 5.Nxd4 simply scoops the wedge and Black has nothing for the pawn. Play 4...Nc6 first — the knight defends d4 and keeps the wedge alive.
albin-countergambit.shortNarration: Nc6 defends the d4 wedge first

sicilian-najdorf.explanation: Against the 6.Bg5 pin, 6...e5? concedes the d5-square for good: the f6-knight is pinned and can't fight for it, so White calmly clamps with a3 and Nd5, enjoying a lasting positional bind on the hole. The flexible 6...e6 keeps d5 covered and the structure sound — the Najdorf's main road.
sicilian-najdorf.shortNarration: e6 keeps d5 covered; e5 leaves a hole

scotch-gambit.explanation: With …d5 Black hit the bishop and the e5-pawn at once. Grabbing the knight with exf6?? walks into …dxc4 — Black wins the bishop and keeps the extra d4-pawn, emerging clearly better even after fxg7 Bxg7. The cool Bb5 instead saves the bishop with tempo by pinning the c6-knight, keeping White's gambit pressure fully alive.
scotch-gambit.shortNarration: Bb5 — pin first, don’t grab f6

scotch-gambit.explanation: Recapturing the d4-pawn with the queen invites …Bc5 and …O-O with gain of tempo, and the exposed queen hands Black the initiative. Recapture with Nxd4 instead — the knight centralises safely and keeps White's development lead.

Kicking the e4-knight with f3?? rips open White's own king before castling and drops material to the loose centre. Just castle: O-O tucks the king away and connects the rooks, after which White calmly attends to the e4-knight.
scotch-gambit.shortNarration: O-O — castle, don’t play f3 yet

vienna-gambit.explanation: Snatching the e5-pawn with Nxe5 is the natural move a quarter of players choose — but after …Qe7 the pin wins the knight back and equalises. Qe2 first keeps the pawn defended and the initiative: White stays a healthy edge ahead with the f-file and the big centre.
vienna-gambit.shortNarration: Qe2 — defend first, don’t grab e5

vienna-gambit.explanation: With the bishop on c5 eyeing f2, the greedy d3 (hitting the e4-knight) runs into …Qh4+ and …O-O with a raging attack on the white king. Qe2 calmly defends, unpins, and prepares O-O-O — White keeps the extra central pawn without exposing the king.

danish-gambit.explanation: When Black returns a pawn with …d5, the right reply is exd5 — open the centre while White is the better-developed side. Pushing e5 instead surrenders the centre and the initiative; the once-menacing pawns become weak and Black equalises comfortably.
danish-gambit.shortNarration: exd5 — open the centre, don’t push e5

danish-gambit.explanation: Black's queen has drifted to c4 — pounce with Bxc6+! The zwischenzug check forces …bxc6 (wrecking Black's queenside) before White trades queens on the next move, emerging with the better structure. The routine Qe2+ instead just trades and lets Black recapture cleanly.

smith-morra-gambit.explanation: Recapture on c3 with the knight — Nxc3 is the whole point of the Morra: rapid development and open lines for the gambit pawn. Taking with bxc3 instead doubles White's pawns, blunts the attack, and leaves White simply a pawn down with nothing to show for it.

Grabbing the b5-pawn with Bxb5?? hangs the bishop to …axb5, since the a6-pawn defends b5 — a clean piece for a pawn. Retreat to Bb3 instead, keeping the bishop trained on the a2-g8 diagonal and f7 where the Morra's pressure lives.
smith-morra-gambit.shortNarration: Bb3 — keep the diagonal, b5 is poisoned

marshall-attack.explanation: The Marshall attacker is hunting the white king, but Qxh2+?? is a mirage — after Kxh2 Black has simply given the queen for one pawn. The quiet Qh3 is the killer: it keeps the queen on the attack, threatens mate ideas on g2, and ties White in knots.
marshall-attack.shortNarration: Qh3 — keep the queen, don’t take h2

marshall-attack.explanation: The greek-gift Bxh2+ is premature here — after Kxh2 there is no follow-up and Black is just a piece down. Bring the queen out first with Qh4, eyeing h2 and the kingside; only with the pieces coordinated does the Marshall attack catch fire.

stafford-gambit.explanation: This is the whole point of the Stafford — recapture the knight with bxc6! It opens the b-file and the diagonals for Black's pieces and is the only move that justifies the gambit. Forgetting to recapture (…d6) simply leaves Black a piece down for nothing.

englund-gambit.explanation: The famous Englund trap-spring: do NOT grab the rook. After Qxa1?? White plays Qc3 and the black queen is trapped in the corner. The killer is Bxc3! — pinning and winning, since Qxc3 walks into …Qc1 mate. Greed loses; the pin wins.
englund-gambit.shortNarration: Bxc3 — pin and win, not Qxa1

englund-gambit.explanation: Don't settle for the queen trade — it's mate! Qc1# ends the game on the spot: the queen drops to c1, the king has no escape and nothing covers the square. Trading with Qxc3+ throws away the whole point of the trap.

pro-ericrosen-stafford.explanation: When White trades on c6, the recapture matters enormously. dxc6 takes toward the centre and opens the d-file for the queen and the c8-to-h3 diagonal for the light bishop — those open roads ARE the compensation for the pawn. bxc6 instead leaves the queen and light bishop boxed in behind their own pawns, and the gambit loses all its point. Always recapture toward the centre.

It is tempting to jump straight to g4 to hit f2 — but here White can simply chase the knight or trade it off, and the attack fizzles. Rosen plays h5 FIRST: it opens the h-file for the rook AND takes away the squares White would use to harass the knight on g4. Get the move order right — h5, then Ng4 with real force behind it.

Castling kingside here throws the gambit away: it puts the king on exactly the side where Black wants to attack, and it wastes the tempo the initiative depends on. Black is a pawn down — the only justification is the attack, so keep storming: Ng4 brings another piece to f2, and the king will castle queenside later to bring the second rook into the assault. Never go passive in the Stafford.

pro-ericrosen-london.explanation: The cardinal London error: playing e3 first buries the dark-squared bishop behind its own pawn chain, giving you the very bad bishop the London exists to avoid. Always develop the bishop OUT to f4 before locking the chain with e3.

Meeting …Qb6 with b3 permanently weakens the queenside light squares and the c3-square. The clean answer is Na3, rerouting the knight to c4 where it hits the queen with tempo and defends b2 and d4 — no concessions.

Grabbing the b2-pawn is greedy: after Nb5 the knight hits c7 with a fork threat and the queen gets chased to the edge while White develops with huge tempo. Black should just play …d6 and develop — the pawn is poisoned.

pro-ericrosen-sicilian.explanation: Against the Alapin's c3, …Nf6 walks into e5 kicking the knight and handing White a free space advantage. The principled move is …d5, striking the centre before White can build it with d4 — and because c3 blocks Nc3, Black equalises cleanly.

When White trades on c6 in the Rossolimo, recapture toward the centre with …dxc6: it keeps a healthy structure and opens the d-file and the c8-bishop's diagonal. …bxc6 leaves you with chronically weak doubled c-pawns and nothing to show for them.

pro-ericrosen-qgd.explanation: In the Carlsbad, …Be7 is passive — the bishop does nothing on e7. Develop it actively to d6, eyeing h2, where it powers the kingside counter-attack that is Black's whole plan against White's minority attack.

pro-ericrosen-scandinavian.explanation: Recapturing immediately with …Qxd5 invites Nc3 hitting the queen, and White develops with tempo while Black's queen wanders — the old, passive Scandinavian. The modern …Nf6 regains the pawn with a piece, keeps the queen safe, and gives Black fast, harmonious development.

pro-hikaru-caro-kann.explanation: The French-player's reflex is …e6, but that locks Black's light-squared bishop inside the pawn chain — the very piece the whole Caro-Kann is built to free. Play …Bf5 FIRST, developing the bishop OUTSIDE the chain, and only then …e6. That one difference is why the Caro is a healthier version of the French.

The oldest trap in the book: after Qe2 the natural …Ngf6 walks into Nd6 mate — the e2-queen covers the escape and the d6-knight delivers smothered checkmate. Always slot in …e6 (or …Ndf6) first to give the king luft. Don't be its victim.

pro-hikaru-pirc-modern.explanation: Against the 150 Attack, developing …Nf6 invites White's whole plan — h4-h5 with a kingside storm aimed straight at the knight. The Modern's point is to delay …Nf6 and expand on the queenside FIRST with …b5, grabbing space and aiming the bishop down the long diagonal. Hand White the centre; counter on the wing.

In the Austrian Attack once White closes with e5, the knight has no future on h6 — it sits offside. Instead …Bg4 pins the f3-knight, pressuring White's overextended centre before developing. Activity over passivity: the pin turns White's big centre into a liability.

pro-hikaru-closed-sicilian.explanation: When Black plays the solid …e6 and strikes with …d5, a bishop on c4 runs straight into …d4 / …dxe4 and loses all its bite — it's biting on granite. Against the …e6 structure, switch plans: Bb5 pins the c6-knight and prepares Bxc6 to damage Black's pawns. Bc4 is for the …g6 lines; Bb5 is for …e6.
pro-hikaru-closed-sicilian.shortNarration: vs …e6 and …d5 play Bb5, not Bc4.

pro-hikaru-closed-sicilian.explanation: Pushing d4 opens the position into an Open Sicilian where Black's setup is comfortable and White's f4 is just loose. The Grand Prix is a CLOSED attacking system — keep the centre closed, develop Bc4, and storm with f5. Don't trade your attacking chances for a premature central break.
pro-hikaru-closed-sicilian.shortNarration: Keep it closed — Bc4, not d4.

pro-hikaru-closed-sicilian.explanation: The f5 break is the Grand Prix's knockout punch, but fired too early — before Bc4 and castling — it just drops the f5-pawn or gets exchanged with nothing behind it. Develop the attacking pieces first: Bc4, O-O, THEN f5 with the whole army ready. Timing is everything in a pawn storm.
pro-hikaru-closed-sicilian.shortNarration: Develop first — Bc4 before the f5 break.

pro-hikaru-reti.explanation: In the b3 system the b2-bishop controls e5 and the long diagonal — pushing e4 blocks that diagonal and hands Black central targets. Build with d4 and e3 BEHIND the bishop instead, keeping the diagonal open. The whole point of fianchettoing is to play ON the long diagonal, not to wall it off.
pro-hikaru-reti.shortNarration: d4 keeps the diagonal open; e4 blocks it.

pro-hikaru-reti.explanation: The Ng5 lunge looks aggressive but the knight has no target on g5 and gets kicked straight back by …h6, losing tempo and loosening White's own setup. This is a slow, strategic system — complete development with O-O and play on the long diagonal. Patience beats a premature poke here.
pro-hikaru-reti.shortNarration: Finish developing with O-O; Ng5 gets kicked.

pro-hikaru-nimzo-larsen.explanation: Grabbing the e5-pawn with Bxe5 simply hangs the bishop to …Nxe5 — bishop for a pawn, a losing trade. The b2-bishop's job is to PRESSURE e5 along the diagonal, forcing Black to spend moves defending it, not to capture it. Play e3, develop, and let the long-diagonal bind do the work.

Lashing out with f4 loosens White's king and lets Black hit back with …exf4 or …e4, seizing the centre. The principled move is Bb5, pinning the c6-knight to pile pressure on the e5-pawn the bishop already eyes. Build the bind first; don't crack your own structure open prematurely.
pro-hikaru-nimzo-larsen.shortNarration: Bb5 pins; f4 loosens White's king.

pro-ericrosen-budapest.explanation: After dxe5, …Ne4 is the Fajarowicz — tricky but objectively dubious, and easily neutralised. The sound main line, and the one Rosen plays, is …Ng4: the knight hits the e5-pawn, prepares the quick development with tempo, and keeps all the gambit's traps alive. Pick the move that fights for the pawn AND keeps the initiative.

pro-ericrosen-closed-sicilian.explanation: A quiet g3 setup lets Black equalise comfortably with …Nc6, …g6 and …e5 — exactly the slow Closed Sicilian Black is happy to face. The Grand Prix point is f4: it claims kingside space and commits to the attack. Against the Sicilian, the aggressive f4 is what scores; the passive fianchetto hands Black easy equality.
pro-ericrosen-closed-sicilian.shortNarration: Commit to f4, not the slow g3.

pro-ericrosen-french.explanation: Against the Advance, a passive developing move like …Ne7 lets White consolidate the big centre and slowly squeeze. The French is a counter-attacking defense: …c5 strikes the base of the d4-e5 chain immediately. If you do not hit the chain, you simply have a cramped, lost position — …c5 is not optional, it is the whole point.
pro-ericrosen-french.shortNarration: Hit the chain with …c5, not passive …Ne7.

pro-samayraina-open-sicilian.explanation: After …e5 in the Sveshnikov, retreating Nb3 is passive and lets Black consolidate the centre comfortably. The principled move is Ndb5! — the knight heads for d6 and immediately pressures the d5-hole that …e5 created. Punish the weakness while it's fresh.

pro-samayraina-ruy.explanation: Taking on c6 too early (the Exchange) is playable but throws away the Ruy's main asset — the long-term pin pressure on e5. In the main line we keep the bishop with Ba4, maintaining the tension and the slow build-up that makes the Ruy so dangerous. Only trade on c6 when you have a concrete structural reason.

pro-samayraina-italian.explanation: The Fried Liver attempt with Ng5 leads to wild, heavily-analysed complications where one slip loses. Unless you've memorised the lines, the calm d3 is far better — it transposes to the quiet Pianissimo where understanding beats theory and you keep all the chances with none of the risk.
pro-samayraina-italian.shortNarration: Calm d3, not the sharp Ng5.

pro-samayraina-french-white.explanation: In the Exchange French, developing the bishop passively to e7 wastes its potential. The active …Bd6 (mirroring White) points at h2 and keeps Black's chances alive. In a symmetrical structure, passive piece placement hands the opponent the initiative — always develop to the most active square.

pro-samayraina-caro-white.explanation: After the Panov's exd5, recapturing with the queen drops it into the centre where Nc3 chases it with tempo, handing White a big development lead. The correct recapture is …cxd5, keeping the structure sound. Never let your queen be a target in the opening.

pro-samayraina-open-e5.explanation: The Bird's Defense …Nd4 is a sideline that gives White an easy game after Nxd4 exd4 d3. The principled main line is …a6, the Morphy move — it questions the bishop and keeps all of Black's options open. Play the most-tested move and reach the rich Closed Ruy structures.

pro-samayraina-sicilian-black.explanation: …g6 commits to a Dragon, walking into the dangerous Yugoslav Attack (Be3, f3, Qd2, O-O-O, h4-h5). The Najdorf's …a6 is more flexible — it controls b5, keeps the kingside intact, and decides the setup only after White shows their hand. Flexibility is the Najdorf's great strength.

pro-samayraina-scandi.explanation: The greedy …Qe5+ (eyeing the e-file) just loses time after Be2 or Nge2, and the queen gets chased again. The modern, super-solid retreat is …Qd8 — the queen returns home completely safe and Black builds a sound Caro-like structure. Don't keep the queen exposed in the opening.
